text_html: A 42-year-old man comes to the office because of a 15-year history of episodes of nosebleeds that occur every few days. Application of manual pressure for 2 minutes stops the bleeding. He has a history of one episode of gastrointestinal bleeding 3 years ago and was found to have iron deficiency anemia at that time, which was treated with iron supplementation. His mother had a history of similar symptoms and died of a hemorrhagic stroke 20 years ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s condition?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: This patient’s long history of epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding along with telangiectasias is consistent with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), which results from an abnormality in angiogenesis.

Evaluation: HHT classically presents with recurrent spontaneous epistaxis beginning in adolescence and mucocutaneous telangiectasias. HHT results from loss-of-function mutations affecting signaling pathways that are critical for transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) signaling in vascular endothelial cells. These mutations result in abnormal angiogenesis, producing blood vessels that are prone to bleeding.

Definition: Mutations affecting the TGF-β signaling pathway in HHT lead to abnormal blood vessel development and fragile, dilated vessels. These defects result in telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations that allow direct artery-to-vein connections, causing bleeding and shunting. Diagnosis of HHT involves a clinical assessment using the Curaçao criteria, which includes recurrent epistaxis, multiple telangiectasias, visceral arteriovenous malformations, and a first-degree relative with HHT. If clinical features are inconclusive, genetic testing can provide further definitive diagnosis.

Prevention: HHT cannot be prevented as it is an inherited autosomal dominant disorder. However, early diagnosis allows appropriate screening and preventive treatment to decrease complications in affected patients and their family members.

Treatment: Treatment for HHT includes iron replacement for iron deficiency anemia and local ablative procedures for arteriovenous malformations. There is no medical treatment that addresses the underlying disorder.

Differential: This patient’s differential diagnosis includes inherited bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease and causes of telangiectasias such as ataxia telangiectasia. However, his history and presentation are most consistent with HHT.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: Decreased intercellular adhesion is incorrect. Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from intercellular adhesion due to absence or abnormal function of the glycoprotein Ib receptor. Bernard-Soulier syndrome presents with enlarged platelets and coagulopathy.

Choice C: Defective platelet activation is incorrect. Thrombasthenia is a bleeding disorder that results from decreased platelet activation.

Choice D: Deficiency of coagulation factors is incorrect. Hemophilia A and hemophilia B are hereditary coagulation factor deficiencies that result in increased bleeding risk. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with HHT. Hemophilia would not result in the presence of telangiectasias.

Choice E: Exposure to a toxin is incorrect. This patient has a 15-year history of bleeding; toxin exposure would only cause bleeding during the duration of action of, and recovery from, toxic exposure. Toxins that cause bleeding could include coumarin derivatives (eg, rat poison).
